item.title: Fintech Startups To Watch: Startups That Caught Our Eye In October
item.dc:creator: Gaurav Bagur
item.description: The question of when India’s Unified Payments Interface (UPI) will finally be monetised has remained at the centre of the…
item.content:encoded:
The question of when India’s Unified Payments Interface (UPI) will finally be monetised has remained at the centre of the fintech industry’s conversations over the past month. 

The debate intensified after the National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI) deferred the introduction of merchant discount rate (MDR) charges on select UPI person-to-merchant (P2M) transactions.

Earlier reports suggested that the rollout could be pushed to January 2027. However, the framework now appears likely to be introduced after Diwali, with the industry awaiting a final announcement.

Under the proposed framework, eligible P2M UPI transactions above ₹2,000 would attract an MDR fee of 0.40%, capped at ₹300 per transaction. The proposal has drawn resistance from retail traders, who argue that the charges would add to their operating costs.

The All India Mobile Retailers Association (AIMRA) and the All India Consumer Products Distributors Federation (AICPDF) also called for a ‘No UPI Day’ protest, but eventually withdrew the proposal following a meeting with finance minister Nirmala Sitharaman. Separately, advocate Anjan Datta filed a public interest litigation (PIL) challenging the policy in the Supreme Court. The apex court, however, declined to stay the proposed MDR charges.

Meanwhile, UPI transaction volumes and values declined month-on-month (MoM) in September. The number of transactions fell nearly 1.8% to 24.07 Bn, while their cumulative value dropped 1.5% to ₹29.37 Lakh Cr.

However, the decline that followed August was met with an all-time high in monthly transaction volumes. Average daily UPI transactions increased to 802 Mn in September from 791 Mn in August, while the average daily transaction value rose to ₹97,913 Cr from ₹96,205 Cr.

For banks, payment companies and third-party application providers (TPAPs), the proposed MDR framework could open up a new revenue stream in a market where monetisation has remained a persistent challenge. 

Meanwhile, the uncertainty around the rollout has also weighed on listed fintech companies. Reports of a delay in MDR implementation triggered declines in the stocks of Paytm, Pine Labs and MobiKwik, underlining the potential impact of UPI monetisation on the broader payments ecosystem.

As the industry awaits greater clarity on the future of UPI and the economics of digital payments, we are back with the October edition of Five Fintech Startups To Watch. This monthly series spotlights startups operating in some of the most promising and fast-evolving segments of India’s fintech ecosystem.

With that, here are five interesting ventures that caught our attention this month.

Editor’s Note: The list below is not a ranking of any kind. Startups have been listed alphabetically.

Credfix | Helping Distressed Borrowers

Falling behind on loan repayments can quickly turn into a stressful cycle of recovery calls, mounting worries about credit scores and uncertainty over what to do next. For many borrowers, negotiating with lenders, exploring settlement options and dealing with legal notices can be just as daunting as the debt itself.

In India’s about $200 Mn debt collection software market, Bengaluru-based Credfix is trying to help borrowers deal with debt through an AI-powered platform. Founded in 2025 by Ranjan Agarwal, Neeraj Kulkarni and Ayush Kedia, Credfix helps borrowers understand their financial situation and explore ways to repay or settle their outstanding loans. It also helps lenders recover money from borrowers who are struggling to pay.

The startup currently serves over 2 Lakh borrowers with total outstanding debt of more than ₹4,000 Cr. Around 40% of its users are from tier II and tier III cities.

Credfix combines AI-powered tools with human support to help borrowers at different stages of the debt repayment process. Its Risi AI assistant offers guidance on available settlement options, responding to legal notices and dealing with recovery agents.

The startup also helps borrowers negotiate one-time settlements, where lenders agree to close a loan for less than the total amount owed. In addition, it explains borrowers’ rights and provides step-by-step guidance on rebuilding their CIBIL scores after settling their loans.

FOLO | Bringing Entire Wealth Into One View

A person’s wealth is often spread across multiple bank accounts, investments, insurance policies and other assets. Keeping track of everything can make it difficult to know how much they own, how much they owe and how their overall financial position is changing.

FOLO, short for Family Of Loved Ones, is trying to solve this problem with an app that brings a person’s financial information together in one place. Founded in 2022 by Munmun Desai and Vishal Purohit, the startup operates in India’s $171.2 Bn wealth management market, which is projected to grow at over 10.6% annually over the next eight years. It has raised over $2.9 Mn in funding so far.

FOLO is a SEBI-registered investment adviser that collects financial information from more than 650 sources, including bank accounts, mutual funds, stocks, fixed deposits, property, loans, credit cards and insurance policies. This gives users a consolidated view of their assets and liabilities, without having to manually track everything.

The platform uses the account aggregator framework to access financial information in a read-only mode, with users’ consent. It also allows users to share selected financial details with up to four trusted individuals, such as family members or financial advisers, without revealing their account login details.

Beyond tracking wealth, FOLO offers an offline service, called LYNC, to help users transfer their assets to nominees after their death.

The startup claims to have connected assets worth more than ₹20,000 Cr on its platform and crossed 1 Lakh app downloads.

Spring Street | Making Global Investing Accessible To Indians

India’s investors are increasingly looking beyond domestic markets to diversify their bets. However, investing in foreign stocks and other assets can be complicated, with hurdles around research, money transfers, taxes and regulatory compliance.

Founded in 2026 by Nishant Bansal, Spring Street is building a platform that gives Indian residents and non-resident Indians (NRIs) access to international markets through managed investment portfolios. Backed by Nexus Venture Partners, the startup is targeting a growing appetite for overseas investments. Indian residents remitted around $2.6 Bn (₹22,000 Cr) for overseas investments in FY26, up nearly 56% from $1.69 Bn in FY25.

Its flagship product, Prisma, offers professionally managed portfolios investing in international stocks, bonds and commodities. These portfolios provide exposure to markets across North America, Europe, Asia and Latin America, with options tailored to investors’ risk appetites and financial goals.

Spring Street also handles overseas investing, from onboarding and identity verification to remittance paperwork and investment tracking. To facilitate investments under the Reserve Bank of India’s Liberalised Remittance Scheme (LRS), the startup has partnered with GIFT City-based ViewTrade, which is regulated by the International Financial Services Centres Authority (IFSCA). ViewTrade acts as the broker and custodian.

Spring Street charges an annual portfolio management fee of 1.25% to 1.50% of assets managed, depending on the portfolio, with no additional commissions on individual trades. Investors need to start with a minimum investment of $500.

UpTik | Unlocking Invoice Discounting For SMEs

Small and medium enterprises (SMEs) often struggle with cash flow when customers take weeks or months to pay their invoices. This can leave businesses short of money to cover everyday expenses or fund their next order. At the same time, retail investors looking beyond traditional investment products have limited access to opportunities linked to short-term business financing.

Hyderabad-based UpTik is trying to bridge this gap by connecting investors with businesses seeking working capital. Founded in 2025 by Ainampudi Vinod Varma, Mudunuri Dileep Varma, Phanindra Kumar and Uma Mukesh Ponduru, the startup allows businesses to raise funds against unpaid invoices, while investors can earn returns when those invoices are paid.

UpTik claims to have grown its assets under management (AUM) from ₹6.5 Cr in March 2026 to over ₹25 Cr in September 2026. Monthly disbursements also rose from ₹3.6 Cr to ₹13.3 Cr over the same period.

Through its platform, UpTik offers retail investors, HNIs and institutional investors opportunities to finance verified business invoices. The startup lists investment opportunities with defined tenures and provides details about the underlying transactions, expected returns and associated risks. 

Investors must complete KYC checks, while each deal undergoes due diligence and legal screening. Users can also track their investments and request withdrawals of returns to an in-app wallet.

UpTik provides additional protection against defaults on select deals. The startup plans to expand beyond invoice discounting into other alternative investments, including corporate bonds and startup investments.

Zomint | Democratising Wealth Management

While wealthy individuals can hire wealth managers to guide their financial decisions, professionals and families with smaller portfolios often have to navigate investment choices on their own.

Chandigarh-based Zomint aims to bridge this gap by helping professionals and families manage their wealth through personalised financial advice. Founded in 2025 by Aman Mittal and Shavir Bansal, the wealthtech startup draws on Bansal’s earlier venture, the personal finance content platform Bekifaayati, which claims a community of over 50 Lakh and more than 80 Lakh monthly views. This audience has also helped Zomint build its customer base.

According to a market assessment published in an NSE-hosted document in November 2025, India’s investment and wealth management sector had an estimated annual addressable market of ₹1.1 Lakh Cr in FY25. The assessment projects this to reach ₹2.2 Lakh Cr to ₹2.6 Lakh Cr by FY30.

The startup assigns each customer a dedicated financial expert who uses AI tools and research to track investments, recommend suitable mutual funds and guide financial decisions over time. Its relationship managers currently serve more than 250 families each.

Zomint lets customers start with a monthly systematic investment plan (SIP) of ₹25,000 or a lump-sum investment of ₹5 Lakh. Its investment options include equity, debt and hybrid mutual funds, gold and silver funds, and global investment products available through GIFT City.

Beyond helping customers choose investments, Zomint actively monitors their portfolios and can recommend changes based on market conditions, developments affecting individual funds or shifts in customers’ financial circumstances. This allows the startup to offer ongoing guidance rather than one-time investment recommendations.

Edited by Shishir Parasher

Meesho’s Q2 Snapshot

Meesho inched closer to profitability in Q2 FY27. The quarter saw the ecommerce giant rein in its losses, scale its revenues and improve its contribution margins. Yet macroeconomic volatility and loss-making new bets continued to weigh on its bottom line in Q2. 

Here’s a quick look at Meesho’s Q2 FY27 numbers: 

  • Net loss narrowed 68% YoY to ₹132.4 Cr 
  • Operating revenue rose 34% YoY to ₹4,131.6 Cr
  • Total expenses increased 24% YoY to ₹4,382.3 Cr 

The Marketplace Engine: As usual, Meesho’s core marketplace vertical accounted for the biggest chunk of its revenues in Q2, driven by a growing base of active transacting users and higher order frequency. What also came in handy were expanding margins, optimised logistics, strong user retention across Tier II+ markets and AI-driven automation. 

Costly New Bets: On the flip side, Meesho’s newer initiatives – hyperlocal logistics, digital financial services and AI services – continued to widen their losses. However, revenues from these emerging businesses also rose sharply. The management sees faster deliveries, logistics efficiencies and AI eventually making these ventures more viable going forward.

In line with this, the listed company has invested an additional ₹75 Cr in Meesho Grocery to support its growth and financial requirements.

The Festive Cheer: Going forward, critics will be closely watching Meesho’s Q3 results as the quarter will capture a bigger portion of the company’s festive sales. This is because its ‘Mega Blockbuster Sale’ shifted from Q2 last fiscal to Q3 this year. The leadership expects Q3 growth to appear stronger, although it will require continued elevated spending during the Diwali period.

As the ecommerce giant continues its march towards profitability, here’s how Meesho fared on the financial front in Q2 FY27… 

From The Editor’s Desk

Info Edge CEO Quits After 27 Years

  • Info Edge founder Sanjeev Bikhchandani will take over as executive vice chairman, MD and group CEO from December 3, 2026, succeeding Hitesh Oberoi, who is stepping down after nearly 27 years in a full-time executive role.
  • Oberoi will remain on the board as a non-executive, non-independent director. He cited plans to focus more on education, entrepreneurship, investing, philanthropy and family.
  • Info Edge’s consolidated net profit surged 87% YoY to ₹649.8 Cr in Q2 FY27, while revenue from operations rose 12.2% to ₹903.9 Cr. A 164.8% jump in other income to ₹428.4 Cr also contributed to profit growth.

Cognizant Eyes Sarvam Stake

  • The AI giant is in talks to raise $300 Mn at a valuation of $3.5 Bn to $4 Bn, more than double its previous valuation of $1.5 Bn just four months ago.
  • The potential investment will make Cognizant the second IT services major to back Sarvam after HCLTech, as IT firms look to strengthen AI capabilities amid growing automation risks to traditional outsourcing.
  • Sarvam is expanding its enterprise AI business, with customers including LIC, SBI Life, IDFC First Bank, Tata Capital and CRED. It is also pursuing AI projects in the defence sector through an MoU with the defence ministry’s Headquarters Integrated Defence Staff.

Astrotalk’s Profit Zooms 10X In FY26

  • The spiritual tech startup’s consolidated net profit jumped nearly 10X to ₹222 Cr in FY26, while operating revenue grew 55% YoY to ₹1,823 Cr. Profit before tax nearly quadrupled to ₹296 Cr.
  • International revenue surged 2.6X to ₹621 Cr, contributing 34% of operating revenue. Ecommerce revenue more than quadrupled to ₹166 Cr as Astrotalk Store expands beyond astrology consultations into spiritual products.
  • Cash flow from operations rose 21% to ₹229 Cr, while year-end cash and investments increased 41% to ₹917 Cr. The startup said it funded its expansion through internal cash flows. Astrotalk entered the unicorn club in August at a $1 Bn valuation following an ESOP buyback.

Moms Home’s Quick Commerce Bet

  • Jaipur-based baby essentials brand grew quick commerce revenue from around ₹1 Cr in FY25 to ₹10 Cr in FY26, accounting for nearly 30% of its ₹35 Cr top line. Monthly sales have since approached ₹5 Cr, with the brand selling around 45,000 kits a month.
  • Contribution margins have declined from 20-25% initially to 10-15%, amid inventory and replenishment challenges. The babycare brand has adapted by focusing on curated newborn and gifting kits and assembling products based on demand to reduce the risk of unsold inventory.
  • Moms Home aims to generate ₹30 Cr in quick commerce revenue in FY27 and expects the channel to contribute up to 50% of overall revenue in the next 15-18 months. It is also exploring a $3 Mn fundraise and plans to strengthen direct-to-consumer deliveries as it looks to reduce dependence on third-party platforms.

CarTrade’s Mixed Q2

  • The automotive classifieds company reported a consolidated net profit of ₹66 Cr in Q2 FY27, up 3% YoY and 16.2% QoQ. Meanwhile, operating revenue grew 10.2% YoY to ₹213.1 Cr and 5.9% sequentially. 
  • Including other income of ₹23.1 Cr, total income stood at ₹236.2 Cr. Total expenses increased 6% YoY to ₹150.8 Cr but declined 0.9% QoQ. 
  • The September quarter had no exceptional expenses, unlike the preceding quarter, which included a ₹3.1 Cr charge linked to salary restructuring under the new labour codes.

Inc42 Markets

Inc42 Startup Spotlight

Can Firi Make Beauty Shopping Less Overwhelming?

Beauty shoppers today have thousands of products to choose from. But more choices often mean more time spent researching what actually works. Firi is trying to solve this with its opinionated online store that uses AI to research and stock beauty products and delivers them in minutes.

A Curated Store: Founded in 2026, Firi leverages AI agents to analyse online reviews, Reddit discussions, YouTube content and ingredient lists to decide which beauty products to stock. It claims to have so far analysed 50 Mn+ reviews and shortlisted about 3,000 products from more than 3 Lakh beauty products globally.

Delivered In Minutes: Firi currently sells skincare, haircare and body care offerings through its only Beauty Studio in parts of Delhi NCR, where it offers deliveries in as little as nine minutes. The startup now plans to add more dark stores in the city before expanding to other markets. 

The Road Ahead: Backed by 360 ONE Asset and Better Capital, Firi plans to now expand into makeup, fragrances and other categories. It is also focusing on scaling its AI-led discovery and fulfilment model. With the homegrown online beauty and personal care market projected to become a $13 Bn opportunity by FY30, can Firi’s AI-led curation model redefine how India shops for beauty products?

item.title: Innodata Lays Off Nearly 550 Employees In India: Report
item.dc:creator: Shrishti Bisht
item.description: US-based Innodata has become the latest company to lay off a big chunk of its staff in India. The AI…
item.content:encoded:
US-based Innodata has become the latest company to lay off a big chunk of its staff in India. The AI services company reportedly axed nearly 550 jobs in the country, nearly 5% of its global workforce. 

According to a termination email reviewed by India Today, the company cited a “ramp-down of the (a) business assignment” as the reason for the layoffs. It also noted that the decision was not linked to individual performance. Simply put, a major client likely pulled the plug on a massive project and Innodata responded by slashing the costs associated with that project. 

The extent of the layoffs, the teams involved and the status of the affected client assignments remain unclear. Inc42 has reached out to the company seeking more clarity on this. The story will be updated on receiving a response.

As per the report, the impacted employees lost access to official IDs and internal systems in the middle of the workday on Monday (October 26), followed by termination emails sent to their personal email accounts.

Many employees had, as usual, reportedly logged in and marked their attendance before reports of layoffs started circulating around lunchtime. As workers sought clarity from their managers and HR teams, access to company systems was gradually withdrawn, the report said.

The email also noted the impacted employee’s full and final settlement had been prepared through a demand draft, which would be handed over once company-assigned assets are returned.

Separately, the AI services company has also reportedly laid off an undisclosed number of employees in the Philippines. 

Founded in 1988, US-based Innodata provides data engineering and AI services, including data labelling, model training, evaluation and safety testing. The company lists Google, Microsoft and Amazon among its clients. Innodata had 10,107 employees globally at the end of December 2025.

The development comes amid a broader wave of workforce adjustments across the tech sector as companies reassess their operations and staffing requirements due to AI-led automation.

Earlier this month, ecommerce giant Amazon reportedly laid off at least 100 employees in India as part of its latest global job cuts. Before that, it was also reported that Oracle was preparing to lay off thousands of employees globally, with India expected to be among the markets affected by the planned cuts.

item.title: Exclusive: Holiday Tribe In Talks To Raise ₹50 Cr From RPSG Capital Ventures, Others

item.description: Traveltech startup Holiday Tribe is in talks to raise around ₹50 Cr (about $5.2 Mn) in a fresh funding round,…
item.content:encoded:
Traveltech startup Holiday Tribe is in talks to raise around ₹50 Cr (about $5.2 Mn) in a fresh funding round, with RPSG Capital Ventures among the prospective investors, sources told Inc42.

The startup is actively engaging with the investment firm, the sources said. However, the round is yet to be finalised, and its size and investor participation could change as discussions progress.

Queries sent to Holiday Tribe and RPSG Capital Ventures did not elicit a response by the time of publication.

Founded in 2022 by Anshu Sharma and Chirag Goyal, both former MakeMyTrip executives, Holiday Tribe offers customised holiday packages. The startup combines AI-powered planning with travel experts to provide itinerary recommendations, bookings, and support for family holidays, honeymoons, luxury trips, and group travel.

Its platform features a planning tool called Avni and lists domestic and international destinations, including Kerala, Bali, Dubai, Japan, Vietnam, and several European markets. Customers can also seek customised quotes through its travel advisors.

Holiday Tribe previously raised ₹25 Cr in a pre-Series A round last year. The round comprised equity and debt. Powerhouse Ventures led the fundraise, with participation from GSF and undisclosed angel investors. Before that, the startup raised ₹5.4 Cr in seed funding in 2024.

At the time of the pre-Series A fundraise, Holiday Tribe said it would invest in AI capabilities for personalisation, itinerary optimisation, and customer assistance, while expanding its supplier base in emerging destinations. Its deployment plans for the proposed fresh round are not yet known.

RPSG Capital Ventures, part of the RP-Sanjiv Goenka Group, is an early-stage consumer investment firm focused on businesses across food and beverages, personal care, and lifestyle goods and services.

Investors Back Customised Holiday Platforms

Holiday Tribe’s funding talks come amid investments in startups building customised holiday planning and booking services.

In July, Gurugram-based 30 Sundays raised ₹61 Cr in a Series A round led by Bessemer Venture Partners, with participation from Info Edge Ventures and Eximius Ventures.

30 Sundays offers itinerary planning, bookings, and on-trip support for outbound Indian travellers, primarily targeting couples. It said the capital would help strengthen its AI capabilities, expand its engineering team, and enter markets including Georgia, Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan, and the Philippines.

The startup uses AI across lead qualification, itinerary creation, follow-ups, and reservations. At the time of the fundraise, it claimed an annualised gross booking value run rate of about ₹200 Cr across Bali, Vietnam, the Maldives, and Thailand.

Established travel platforms are also expanding their holiday offerings. Earlier this month, TravClan raised $5 Mn through a mix of equity and debt, with Flipkart and August One investing in equity and Trifecta Capital providing debt.

The partnership is intended to help Cleartrip and Flipkart Travel expand their curated international holiday packages and on-ground support. TravClan works with more than 15,000 travel agents to customise and book packages, hotels, and activities.

item.title: Why Indian AI Founders Are Eyeing Silicon Valley And What They Risk Leaving Behind

item.content:encoded:
When AI-powered sales intelligence startup Reo.Dev raised $11.3 Mn in July 2026, its priorities reflected a growing reality for Indian startups building for global markets.

The company planned to deploy fresh capital towards expanding sales and marketing operations in the US, which already accounted for nearly two-thirds of its revenue. Yet most of its approximately 75-member workforce remained in India.

Reo.Dev is not alone in operating across these two markets. Bengaluru- and San Francisco-based Coreworks AI raised $5 Mn earlier this year to develop its enterprise AI platform. More recently, RapidCanvas secured $29 Mn to expand its go-to-market and field AI engineering teams across India, the US and Brazil.

These companies illustrate the increasingly international nature of India’s AI startup ecosystem, where the markets founders sell into, the teams they build and the locations from which they operate do not necessarily overlap.

The momentum is backed by capital.

According to Inc42’s Indian Tech Startup Funding Report, Q3 2026, Indian AI startups raised $438 Mn during the July–September quarter, a 265% year-on-year increase. With $676 Mn raised in the first half, cumulative funding for the first nine months of 2026 crossed $1.1 Bn.

As more startups pursue global AI opportunities, however, an important question is emerging. Does getting closer to Silicon Valley necessarily make an Indian AI startup more competitive?

For Suhas Motwani, cofounder of The Product Folks, a global community of product professionals and builders, the answer is more complicated than a change of address.

“The corridor is real, and for a lot of founders it is useful,” says Motwani. “The harder question is what gets built on each side of it, and what gets lost when the move happens too early.”

Why Silicon Valley Is Becoming Harder To Ignore

The attraction of Silicon Valley extends well beyond fundraising, which was the case even at the height of the Indian SaaS boom.

For AI startups, just like SaaS startups before them, proximity to potential enterprise customers, experienced operators, specialised talent and the wider AI ecosystem can shorten the distance between product development and commercial validation.

That matters particularly for startups building enterprise AI products, where customer discovery often requires understanding complex workflows, procurement processes, security requirements and the commercial value of automation.

As Inc42 previously explored in its analysis of enterprise AI sales, winning enterprise customers is no longer simply about demonstrating technical capabilities. Startups must identify decision-makers, prove measurable returns and navigate the operational risks associated with deploying AI in live business environments.

For companies whose largest potential customers are American enterprises, building those relationships from thousands of kilometres away can introduce additional challenges.

Physical presence can create opportunities for more frequent customer interactions, closer feedback loops and a better understanding of how enterprise buying decisions are made.

Motwani believes this proximity can be particularly useful in a sector where product capabilities, customer expectations and competitive positioning are evolving rapidly. But there is an important distinction between using Silicon Valley to accelerate learning and treating relocation itself as a competitive advantage.

“A low barrier to raising in the Bay is very different from a low barrier to building a durable company,” he says. “The move itself is cheap. The compounding effects are not.”

The challenge for founders is to determine whether their company genuinely needs a physical presence in the US, and what business outcomes that presence is expected to deliver.

How AI Is Changing The India–US Equation

The India–US technology corridor is not new. Indian SaaS companies have spent years building products and engineering teams at home while selling to enterprise customers abroad.

However, AI is changing the economics of that relationship.

The cost and complexity of developing frontier AI models continue to demand enormous capital, computing infrastructure and specialised talent. At the same time, access to increasingly capable models is making it possible for smaller teams to build AI-powered applications without developing the underlying technology themselves.

The distinction is becoming more visible as the global AI industry enters a new phase.

On 26 October, Anthropic publicly filed its registration statement for a proposed US initial public offering. The Claude maker reported approximately $16.3 Bn in revenue during the first half of 2026, compared with about $1.2 Bn in the corresponding period last year, illustrating the rapid commercial expansion of the frontier AI industry. Its proposed listing also comes amid questions over the enormous capital requirements and long-term economics of building advanced AI models.

For Indian founders, the implications extend beyond the public market performance of companies such as Anthropic.

While frontier AI development remains heavily capital-intensive, application-layer startups can increasingly build on models developed elsewhere, allowing them to direct more resources towards solving specific customer problems.

This distinction is particularly relevant to India. According to the Google × Inc42 Bharat AI Startups Report, 2026, 90% of funded Indian AI startups covered in its analysis operate at the application layer.

However, access to powerful models also means that technological capabilities can become easier for competing startups to replicate. A sophisticated AI feature, by itself, may no longer constitute a lasting competitive advantage.

What becomes harder to replicate is a startup’s understanding of its customers, its integration into their workflows, its distribution network and the trust it builds through repeated use.

This is where the India–US corridor takes on a different significance.

For application-layer startups, being close to Silicon Valley can offer access to frontier AI developments, customers and distribution networks. But the ability to build quickly, experiment cost-effectively and develop products for demanding users can remain rooted in India.

The opportunity is no longer just about exporting Indian engineering capabilities to the US. It is about determining which parts of an AI business need to operate closer to the technology frontier, which need to be closer to customers, and where the startup can build its strongest competitive advantage.

Knowing The Risks

For much of the past decade, Indian technology startups have competed globally by combining engineering talent, leaner operating structures and access to international markets.

AI is changing the economics of building software, but it has not eliminated the importance of these advantages.

Moving an entire founding or engineering team to San Francisco can significantly increase operating costs, particularly when the startup is still experimenting with products, pricing and its target customer segment.

More importantly, an early relocation can affect the company’s product development process.

Founders who move away from their engineering teams may find themselves managing critical product decisions across time zones. The resulting separation can make experimentation, communication and decision-making more complex at precisely the stage when startups need to move quickly.

There is also the question of which users influence the product roadmap.

A startup developing AI products for American enterprises may benefit enormously from spending more time with US customers. But the same approach could prove counterproductive for a company building for Indian consumers, small businesses or enterprises with distinctly local requirements.

Motwani argues that the environment in which a startup develops its earliest products can influence the capabilities it prioritises and the problems it learns to solve.

India, for instance, exposes AI products to considerable variation in languages, devices, connectivity, user behaviour and willingness to pay.

A product designed around affluent, English-speaking users with reliable connectivity may not necessarily work as effectively for consumers using regional languages, shared devices or less predictable networks.

These constraints can force teams to improve reliability, usability and cost efficiency much earlier in the product development cycle.

The risk is not that an Indian founder builds for the US. It is that the founder changes markets without deliberately reassessing which customers, capabilities and advantages should shape the business.

An Opportunity Too Large To Overlook

The case for maintaining a strong presence in India is also increasingly supported by the size of the domestic opportunity.

According to the Google × Inc42 Bharat AI Startups Report, 2026, India’s AI market is projected to reach $126 Bn by 2030.

Enterprise AI expenditure is estimated to grow from $11 Bn in 2025 to $71 Bn by 2030, while consumer AI expenditure is projected to rise from $13 Bn to $55 Bn over the same period.

For application-layer startups, this represents a significant opportunity to build products that address specific customer problems, integrate into existing workflows and earn sustained adoption.

There are, however, important differences between market opportunity and commercial readiness.

India was already the world’s second-largest market for AI application downloads in 2024, accounting for 177 Mn downloads. Yet the Bharat AI report estimated consumer AI monetisation at just $12 Mn during that period.

In other words, significant user adoption does not automatically translate into strong monetisation.

For Indian AI founders, this creates two different opportunities. The US offers access to enterprise customers with established software budgets, while India offers a large and diverse market in which startups can build products around local workflows and underserved customer segments.

Choosing between them should depend on the problem being solved, rather than the assumption that one market is inherently superior.

There are also alternative routes to global customers that do not require startups to abandon their Indian operating base.

An earlier analysis published on Inc42 examined how India’s Global Capability Centres (GCCs) could become an important route to multinational enterprise buyers, offering Indian AI startups access to global workflows and potential decision-makers within the country itself.

The major implication is that access to international customers does not always require shifting the entire centre of product development overseas.

The Case For Building Across Two Markets

Rather than viewing Bengaluru and Silicon Valley as competing destinations, Motwani sees merit in founders using the two ecosystems for different purposes.

Through his work with The Product Folks, he has observed differences in the priorities that dominate conversations among founders and product professionals in the two markets.

In San Francisco or the Valley, discussions tend to centre on distribution, pricing and category creation. In Bengaluru, they are often more focused on engineering teams, product positioning, capital efficiency and the immediate challenges of building a sustainable business.

Both perspectives matter.

A startup can build a technically capable AI product in India and still struggle to reach the right international customers. Equally, access to American buyers and investors does not guarantee that the company will develop a defensible product or sustainable business model.

This is where a two-market operating strategy becomes relevant.

For founders serving US enterprises, customer-facing functions may need to be closer to those customers, while product and engineering teams can continue operating from India.

Reo.Dev offers one illustration. As Inc42 reported in July, the startup was expanding its American sales and marketing operations while retaining most of its workforce in India.

But operating across two markets brings its own challenges.

Founders must establish clear ownership of product decisions, maintain communication between customer-facing and engineering teams, and ensure that feedback from international customers translates into improvements rather than endless customisation.

There is also a less visible challenge: access to the right relationships.

Entering a new market requires more than understanding its customers. Founders often need introductions to experienced operators, potential partners, investors, early hires and advisors who understand the practical challenges of building across borders.

Motwani has been working to address some of these gaps through The Founder Folks, an invite-only founder initiative emerging from The Product Folks network.

Built around the India–US corridor, the initiative seeks to connect founders with experienced operators, potential customers and advisors, alongside offering practical guidance on US market entry, fundraising and managing cross-border teams.

Its emphasis reflects a broader challenge in the ecosystem: founders looking to build global businesses need more than access to capital. They also need access to relevant experience, networks and market-specific knowledge.

Ultimately, a US presence can accelerate customer discovery, but whether that learning becomes a competitive advantage depends on how effectively it informs the product being built.

The Real Test Is Product-Market Fit

The debate over where Indian AI startups should operate ultimately connects to a larger challenge facing the sector.

AI has made it easier for startups to develop prototypes, experiment with new capabilities and launch products. But these improvements do not automatically make it easier to build businesses that customers depend on.

Motwani believes founders must distinguish between what an AI product can demonstrate and what users will actually trust it to do.

“The shift from demo to daily use is not about adding features,” he says. “It is about deciding what work a user will actually trust the system to do.”

This distinction becomes particularly relevant when founders enter new markets.

Customer expectations around product reliability, workflow integration, support, pricing and accountability can vary considerably between India and the US.

A product that performs well during a demonstration may still struggle when deployed within an enterprise workflow that requires multiple approvals, integration with legacy systems or verification of AI-generated outputs.

These challenges are becoming more consequential as investor expectations mature.

Inc42’s Q3 2026 investor survey found that 63% of institutional investors surveyed saw some degree of froth in Indian AI startup valuations. At the same time, 39% believed vertical AI applications would capture the greatest value over the next five years.

The findings suggest that while investor interest in AI remains strong, the ability to build commercially viable, differentiated applications will increasingly matter.

For founders, the priority is not simply to reach a larger market. It is to understand which problems customers will pay to solve, how the product fits into their existing processes and whether the business can deliver value consistently.

A startup may need to be in San Francisco to understand those requirements. Another may discover its strongest opportunities by working more closely with Indian enterprises and consumers.

Neither outcome can be determined by geography alone.

Where Will India’s Next Global AI Companies Be Built?

India’s AI startup ecosystem is entering a phase in which global ambitions are becoming more closely intertwined with domestic capabilities.

As frontier AI companies prepare to face greater public market scrutiny, the application layer offers Indian startups an opportunity to participate in the global AI economy without necessarily matching the capital or infrastructure investments of the largest model developers.

But it also raises the competitive bar.

Building products is becoming faster. Access to underlying AI capabilities is expanding. What will distinguish companies is their ability to identify valuable problems, reach the right customers and develop products that become indispensable to their workflows.

Access to US capital, customers and talent can help startups accelerate their growth. At the same time, India’s engineering ecosystem, domestic demand and operating advantages continue to offer meaningful opportunities.

The challenge is to combine those strengths without assuming that a particular operating model will work for every company.

For some founders, relocating to the US will be commercially necessary. For others, maintaining customer-facing teams abroad while building from India may offer a more effective structure. And for startups addressing domestic problems, staying close to Indian users could be fundamental to product-market fit.

The decisions will also evolve as companies grow. What makes sense during initial customer discovery may not be the right structure after a startup finds product-market fit or begins scaling internationally.

Motwani’s argument is that founders should approach these choices as deliberate business decisions rather than signals of ambition.

“The corridor is a tool,” he says. “Like any tool, it rewards the founders who are clear about what they are using it for and punishes the ones who confuse motion for progress.”

As Indian AI companies compete for opportunities on both sides of the Pacific, the differentiator may ultimately be neither their headquarters nor their ability to access Silicon Valley.

It will be whether they can use the strengths of both markets to build products customers value, businesses that endure and competitive advantages that are difficult to replicate.
